primary_source.paper: Ramesh, Bothwell, Ravikumar et al. - Compositional Capabilities of Autoregressive Transformers: A Study on Synthetic, Interpretable Tasks

trace_source: rahul13ramesh/compositional_capabilities, commit 54256841ef5f3af3a39d47288d071f7d04b6da5e, run via synthetic.functions.CreateFunctions + synthetic.generator.SyntheticData.generate_document() exactly as shipped (one Python-3.11-compatibility monkey-patch applied at call time only, not persisted -- see published_trace.txt header).
format_description: A document is 'S' + one T{depth}_{choice} task-token per composition step naming which of {identity, f1, f2, f3} was applied at that depth, then a space-separated sequence of length-seq_len alphabet-token vectors: the initial vector, then one vector per depth step showing that step's function applied elementwise to every position in parallel.
theory_citation: Barrington 1989: composing arbitrary functions [N]->[N] strictly contains composing permutations in S_N (bijections) as a special case, and the S_N word problem alone is NC1-complete for N>=5, so the general (non-bijective) version is at least NC1-hard. Caveat (not softened): non-bijective functions can collapse information (absorbing/fixed points), so the general task need not be NC1-complete the way the pure-bijection S_N case is.

knob.name: function.depth (repo config/gen/conf.yaml)
knob.granularity: integer >=1; tokens per step-vector stay flat across depth (each step prints one fixed-length seq_len vector), total prompt length grows linearly with depth

published_data.paper: Ramesh et al., "Compositional Capabilities of Autoregressive Transformers" (arXiv:2311.12997, ICML 2024)
published_data.metric: in-order and out-of-order generalization accuracy of small transformers/LSTMs trained on function compositions; localization of function-selection (attention) vs. execution (feed-forward) via ablation
published_data.models: small from-scratch transformers and LSTMs (nanoGPT-style 2-layer/1-head per repo's default config/train/conf.yaml; not open-weight LLMs)
published_data.values: not independently re-extracted from the paper's figures/tables in this desk pass; repo's own default net config (n_layer=2, n_head=1, n_embd=120, vocab_size=512) documents the SCALE studied, which is far below gemma2/llama3/qwen2 -- their published accuracy numbers describe from-scratch tiny models, not the open-weight models this desk.json tokenizes for

published_data.paper: Arora, Eyuboglu et al., "Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models" (arXiv:2312.04927)
published_data.metric: multi-query associative recall (MQAR) accuracy vs. model size/architecture (attention vs. gated-convolution vs. hybrid)
published_data.models: small from-scratch transformers, gated-convolution and hybrid architectures (not open-weight LLMs)
published_data.values: not directly comparable: MQAR is one static table with parallel independent queries, not depth-many freshly sampled tables composed serially, so its reported numbers are cited for lineage/contrast only, not as this task's published_data proper

published_data.paper: Barrington, "Bounded-width polynomial-size branching programs recognize exactly those languages in NC1" (1989)
published_data.metric: theoretical basis for the NC1-hardness claim via S_N containment

notes: AMENDMENT 2 pass: no single paper was originally assigned to this task, so the primary_source used here is the closest published analogue actually found and code-verified during sourcing (Ramesh et al. 2024) -- the paper's own repo is also the source of published_trace.txt. IMPORTANT caveat vs. our task's spec definition: the repo's shipped functions are BIJECTIVE lookup tables (np.random.permutation), not arbitrary [N]->[N] functions; the trace and format_description above describe the task exactly AS PUBLISHED (bijections), not our task's intended non-bijective generalization -- see SOURCING.md for the surgery (drop bijection restriction) that would be needed to match our spec's design. Each published document applies the SAME shared function at each depth level to all seq_len=6 alphabet positions in parallel (a length-6 vector), rather than tracking one scalar 'state'; per our task's single-symbol-state definition, state_bits/answer_space above use n_alphabets=10 (log2(10) per position) rather than n_alphabets^seq_len=10^6 for the whole published vector -- flagging this choice since the schema requires one number. A genuine upstream bug was hit and worked around (not fixed in the vendored copy): synthetic/functions.py's get_train_functions() calls random.sample() on a Python `set`, which Python 3.11+ rejects; see published_trace.txt header for the exact runtime-only shim used. Token counts measured with real tokenizer.json files (Qwen/Qwen2-7B from the official HF repo; gemma-2-2b and Llama-3-8B tokenizers are gated on HF, so identical unmodified re-hosts unsloth/gemma-2-2b and NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B were used instead -- see s5_composition/desk.json notes for the same caveat). Notable finding: the published format's subscript-Unicode rendering (X₅, T₀_₃, etc.) is token-INEFFICIENT under all three tokenizers (18.6-25.2 tokens per depth-step for what is semantically a 6-symbol vector), because subscript digit glyphs are rare/multi-byte in these BPE vocabularies -- worth flagging since it means the published human-readable notation is not what should be used if actually prompting an open-weight LLM (a plain-digit rendering, as our own from-scratch task.py design uses, would be far cheaper).
